source.title: Interpolation and Regularization for Causal Learning
source.authors: L. C. Vankadara; Luca Rendsburg; U. von Luxburg; Debarghya Ghoshdastidar

record.tranche_reason: The study theoretically analyzes double descent in causal risk for isotropic linear regression, rather than reproducing the original neural-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites double-descent results from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Its own asymptotic results and stated comparisons of min-norm and optimally regularized ridge estimators are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study derives closed-form asymptotic causal risk for min-norm and ridge linear regression as γ=d/n varies. It shows a double-descent curve in a new setting (causal risk under confounding), with the variance term driving the peak and optimal ridge removing it. This bears on V4 and V6. It is T3 rather than T2 because the setting, causal risk under distribution shift, is new rather than a different method on the original question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with additions. The authors show that min-norm causal risk exhibits double descent, driven by variance. Under ICM (ζ>0) interpolators are never optimal and causal learning needs stronger regularization than statistical learning, resolving Janzing's conjecture. For ζ<0 interpolators can be optimal and the optimal regularization can be negative. For ζ≥1 the optimal regularization is infinite and learning from observational data is harmful.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives asymptotic risk results for a theoretical isotropic linear causal model and compares min-norm interpolation with ridge regularization; it does not reproduce the original neural-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that causal risk and optimal regularization depend on confounding strength ζ; under different ζ regimes, min-norm risk can be better or worse than null risk and optimal regularization can be zero, finite, or infinite.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimal causal regularization increases with confounding strength ζ. It is larger than the optimal statistical regularization for ζ>0, can be zero or negative for ζ<0, and is infinite for ζ≥1 (Theorems 4–6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under distribution shift (confounding), the optimal regularization that removes the double-descent peak differs from the optimal regularization for in-distribution learning.

record.problems: The results concern a simple linear causal model with isotropic covariance; the authors leave arbitrary covariances and more complex or nonlinear causal relationships for future work. The finite-sample risks are shown only in a figure without reported numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported results on the tested versions were omitted. The paper's cited findings from prior work and finite-sample plotted points without stated numerical values were not extracted as separate rows.

untested.parts: All: γ is analysed as a ratio, with no explicit sample-wise result that more data raises risk.
Model classes beyond isotropic linear regression; non-isotropic covariances.
All: no effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Multiple or split peaks; explicit sweeps over label-noise level.

missing.what: Regimes of the min-norm causal risk by S=(1−2ζ)SNR_S. For S>1 min-norm beats null risk in both regimes. For 0≤S≤1 only the underparameterized regime beats null. For S<0 min-norm is always worse than null.
Statistical bias of min-norm increases for γ>1, so the best statistical risk is always underparameterized. Causal bias can decrease for γ>1, giving an optimum at γ→∞, but only when S<0.
Finite-sample risks with d=300 agree with the asymptotic curves.

record.verdict_notes: Purely theoretical study in an asymptotic isotropic linear model; the statistical-risk results are reproduced from Hastie et al. (2019). Double descent is a side result here; the main focus is on regularization under confounding. The γ axis mixes model size and sample size, but the paper frames it as overparameterization.

versions.untested_parts: The study analyzes linear regression, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
It does not vary training sample size near the interpolation threshold while testing its effect on risk.
The analysis is for an isotropic linear causal model and causal risk; it does not establish the claim across other model classes or for statistical risk generally.

Confounding strength is analyzed as a determinant of causal risk and optimal regularization, but the study does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The study analyzes the variance contribution to double descent and the effect of optimal ridge regularization. It does not test multiple or split peaks, or compare outcomes across varied label-noise levels.
No alternative effective-parameter count is used to show that double descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: isotropic linear causal model (1), min-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Analyze asymptotic causal risk as the overparameterization ratio γ=d/n varies.
rows.measure: Limiting causal risk, including its bias and variance contributions.
rows.value: The causal risk curve exhibits double descent: it diverges at the interpolation threshold γ=1 due to the variance term and decreases again for γ>1.
rows.note: The text also describes finite-sample risks with d=300 as well-predicted by the limiting risk, but gives no numerical values for those plotted points.
rows.check: Link and state are fine. The value is a theoretical asymptotic limit (Theorem 2), not an empirical measurement. The baseline is the null-estimator risk ω², shown in Figure 2, not 'not stated'.

source_check.correct: The asymptotic min-norm causal risk diverges at γ=1 and decreases again beyond interpolation. Section 3.2 explicitly identifies the zero estimator as a baseline. Figure 2 labels its excess-risk baseline ω², although the risk definition implies null excess risk r² and total null risk r²+σ̃²+ω².
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Theorem 2 and following paragraph; Section 3.2, opening paragraph and Figures 2–3; Appendix B, proof of Proposition 1.
source_check.problem: The baseline is stated; the result is theoretical, with finite-sample illustration rather than numerical measurements.

rows.subject: isotropic linear causal model (1), min-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the asymptotic causal variance component as γ=d/n varies.
rows.measure: Causal variance component of the risk.
rows.value: The variance term diverges at γ=1 and decreases in the overparameterized regime γ>1; the paper identifies it as the cause of the double-descent behavior.
rows.note: The limiting variance is given in Theorem 2; the text states its behavior across the interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Fine. The variance term is σ̃²γ/(1−γ) for γ<1 and σ̃²/(γ−1) for γ>1, so it scales with the noise σ̃². That supports the noise/variance part of V6.

rows.subject: isotropic linear causal model (1), optimally regularized ridge regression estimator
rows.operation_detail: Compare causal risk across γ for ridge regression with optimal regularization.
rows.value: The optimally regularized ridge risk is always below the min-norm risk; the corresponding generalization curve does not exhibit double descent.
rows.note: The paper states that explicit regularization dampens the variance divergence. The plotted curve is also described in the text.
rows.check: Fine. The text says the absence of double descent under optimal ridge is 'similar to the statistical setting'. The statistical analogue is cited from Hastie et al. and is not the study's own result.

relationships.condition: Isotropic linear causal model, min-norm interpolator, asymptotic causal risk vs γ
relationships.reason: Risk diverges at γ=1 and decreases again for γ>1 (r1). Finite-sample points at d=300 match the limit (Figure 3).
relationships.display_finding: Causal risk diverged at γ=1 and decreased for γ>1, with finite-sample results at d=300 matching the asymptotic limit.

relationships.condition: Causal signal strength S≤1 (including most of the ICM regime); based on the text, Section 3.2 and Figure 2, which no row records
relationships.reason: For 0≤S≤1 the overparameterized regime is always worse than null risk; for S<0 min-norm is always worse than null. The underparameterized side rises monotonically, with no U-shape. So the second descent does not deliver good risk in these regimes.
relationships.display_finding: Overparameterized risk exceeded null risk for 0≤S≤1, minimum-norm risk always exceeded null risk for S<0, and underparameterized risk rose monotonically.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Causal signal strength S≤1 (including most of the ICM regime); based on the text, Section 3.2 and Figure 2, which no row records
source_check.reason: The stated S regimes retain post-interpolation risk improvement. Remaining worse than null risk does not limit V4's stated requirement. The underparameterized monotonic rise qualifies the full curve's shape, but does not remove the second descent. The text does not establish a quantitative meaning for most of the ICM regime.

relationships.condition: Isotropic linear causal model; min-norm vs optimally tuned ridge
relationships.reason: The variance term, proportional to the noise σ̃², causes the divergence at γ=1 (r2). Optimally regularized ridge shows no double descent and is always below the min-norm risk (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Variance proportional to noise σ̃² caused divergence at γ=1, while optimally tuned ridge eliminated double descent and consistently reduced risk below the min-norm estimator.

statements.correction: 0≤S≤1: overparameterized min-norm causal risk exceeds null risk. S<0: min-norm causal risk exceeds null risk throughout. These conditions retain a post-interpolation descent and qualify its usefulness.
